title: Measure information per search directly
why: Nothing measures how much a search teaches. KL(search policy || prior) and value change per search would give a real signal-per-compute number.
test: Log both per position in a short run, and check they separate full searches from cheap ones.

title: Spend search where it can change the result
why: Soft resignation is one narrow case of a general budget question: where does more search change the outcome, and where is it wasted? Framed that way, a yes-or-no concession becomes a search budget that follows how result-affecting the next moves are. There is no direct metric for this yet.
test: Record per-ply root value, KL(search policy || prior) and the value gap between the top two moves in a fresh run. See which of them predicts the result changing, then try a budget that follows it. info-metric is the first step. The dashboard's Reports tab has the ideas report.

title: Connect updates 33 and 36 to the rating graph
why: Both swept the baseline 48-0, so they're only lower bounds. Whether the loop kept improving after them is unknown.
test: Play both against update 45 and update 42. About 40 games each is enough for a large gap.

title: Retest a larger training window
why: 750k beat 250k 51-29 on the small board, while the big board was inconclusive. On 2026-11-03 a 150k window drawn from twice as many generations beat update 23's own window 34-14 on the 38 board. The window at 192 now costs 57 KiB a sample (ownership as bits, ridge as uint8), so 450k trains at a 27 GB peak.
test: Part of value-recipe: arena the 450k window against 150k with the new value labels, on the 38 board.

title: Confirm 128 input as the efficient default
why: 128 searches 2-3.6x faster and scored 30-18 at equal time on the big board. One card plays 18.6k positions/s at 128, 7.4k at 192 and 4.1k at 256, so at 61 Elo a doubling 192 has to beat 128 by about 80 Elo at equal simulations and 256 by about 130.
test: Bootstrap at 128. Train a 192 net from scratch on the same window, then play them at equal time with --opponent-resolution on both boards. Move up once it wins.

title: Train the faster net shapes
why: Fewer blocks, no attention and one norm take the card's ceiling at 128 from 21k positions/s to as much as 62k, but the generator stops gaining near 40k here. Trained nets read 30k for `blocks8` (no policy penalty in a loss screen), 35k for `c_d222_short_n1` (+0.013 KL) and 37k for `m_d111_c22` (+0.022 KL), against a seed spread of 0.003. Early in a run generation speed matters more than play, and any net's games train any shape, so a fast shape could generate first and the run could retrain to a stronger one later. Strength is unmeasured, and these rates need 15 to 20 vCPU per card: on 8 threads of 4 cores `blocks8` lost its whole gain within three minutes.
test: Arena `blocks8`, `c_d222_short_n1` and `m_d111_c22` against the current net at equal time on both boards, about 500 games each. Check a trained one over whole games on 8 vCPU. Checkpoints are in `artifacts/shape-screen/runs/`, and the dashboard's Net shapes tab shows the screen.

title: Cut the CPU work inside inference lanes
why: At 192 the lighter net reads 16.4k positions/s in the generator against a 23k card ceiling, with the CPU 60% idle. Each lane spends 28% of its time packing inputs and materializing outputs, about 1.1 ms a batch, and the card waits. A third lane makes it worse. Applying the board rotation twice per batch also wastes training CPU: the second call only needs the ownership map.
test: Time `input_packing` and `output_materialization` in broker telemetry before and after, then confirm in the generator.

title: Stop the naive generator once its window is full
why: The first update of a fresh run took 64 minutes against about 9, because the naive generator kept all 32 threads while training prepared batches, and it wrote 38 GB of games nobody trains on. Stopping it by hand brought the card straight back.
test: Touch the stop file when the first training starts, and confirm a fresh run's first update finishes in about 10 minutes.

title: Add a score head
why: Final scores have been recorded since 2026-09-24. Margin is richer than win or loss for each game.
test: Add after the ownership test, so the two effects can be told apart.

title: Branch from contested positions
why: sigmago's branch mining was never a fair test: 94% of roots were already decided, because it selected late positions.
test: Offline first: run several continuations from positions with values near even. Stop if they rarely disagree.

title: Revisit randomized search budgets
why: Gave 2.8x the games per hour, but 32 games were discarded and the pilot recipe was rejected. That doesn't rule out the idea.
test: Retry with a recipe that keeps a healthy policy target, judged at equal elapsed compute.

title: Add short-horizon value and opponent-move heads
why: Both can be labelled from existing games, adding more per-position signal.
test: Add one at a time, after ownership.

title: Rate models by game stage and board size
why: One rating hides regressions in the opening or endgame.
test: Extend arena records, and fit a rating per bucket.

title: Ablate the settled input plane
why: It's 92-96% of raster cost, and its strength benefit has never been measured.
test: Train with and without it on one corpus, then arena at equal time.

title: Settle one norm per block
why: About 15% more positions/s at the card's ceiling, with mixed, inconclusive arenas: 86-106 over four small matches. The GPU is the limit on throughput at 128.
test: Train it with the faster net shapes, on the same window as their control.

title: Tree reuse in self-play
why: Arena prototype scored 24-24 and 23-25, and inherited only 9-12 visits per hit.
test: No next step unless search budgets rise a lot.

title: Measure self-play on rented hardware
why: Here 8 vCPU hold 18.1k positions/s at 128 over whole games, at 95% GPU. A faster card needs more, about 5 vCPU per 10k positions/s by extrapolation, and rented hardware has different wake-up costs, so it needs checking on the real box.
test: Run 64 actors at 128 for 7 minutes pinned to half the cores, so games finish, and record positions/s, GPU use and busy cores.

title: Rule regression fixtures
why: Capture cases have no reproducible shared positions.
test: Fixtures for nonlocal capture through pocket closure, disconnected self-capture, opponent removal reviving a group, and simultaneous captures run from one command and are shared with Rust.

title: Browser tests in check.sh
why: A stale UI test went unnoticed because nothing runs these automatically.
test: js-app/tests run headless on Linux. Today they need PowerShell and Windows Chrome.

title: Game-grouped validation
why: Adjacent positions from one game can land on both sides of the split, which makes validation loss optimistic.
test: All positions from one game land in one split, deterministically, tested with overlapping game IDs across shards.

title: Deterministic parallel arena
why: fp16 inference can reorder near-ties as batch shapes change.
test: Decide between bitwise repeatability and bounded stability, then show identical results across repeated fixed-seed runs.

title: Official vertex reach test
why: A bug in this check passes every test. A search of up to 3,000 random games found no position where it alone decides a group.
test: Find such a position, or prove the other two checks cover it.

title: Repetition and ko policy
why: Automated play reaches cycles, but it's unknown whether a strategically meaningful human cycle exists. Rule variants are in docs/history/GAMEPLAY_VARIANTS.md.
test: Find a position players would rationally repeat, then choose between unrestricted repetition, simple ko and superko.

title: Vgo learnings
why: Most runs in artifacts/old/ are in no note. Required before that folder is deleted.
test: Write one line per run in docs/FINDINGS.md: question, result, verdict, trust.

title: Decide the NumPy rasterizer
why: A hand-kept second rasterizer is a correctness risk if Rust covers every case.
test: Delete it unless something still needs the fallback.

title: Adopt 16 value labels per game at value weight 1/16
why: The value head memorized its window: train MAE 0.03, held-out 0.65. On update 23's 450k window, 16 labels per game cut held-out value MSE from 0.99 to 0.58 and lifted the winner from 71% to 79%. Policy KL fell as the value weight dropped and was flat at the no-value bound for weights of 1/8 and below. Stride-8 thinning plus weight decay already beat update 23 116-84. All held-out numbers are one seed.
test: Train two seeds of the recipe on update 23's window and arena them against update 23 and its twin, about 200 games on the 38 board. Then wire --value-labels-per-game 16 --value-weight 0.0625 and the window into bulk-loop.sh.

title: End one-sided pass streaks at random, as a bootstrap
why: 72% of big-board games with a long pass streak ran to the 312-ply cap, so labels read who leads at ply 312. Once a side has passed 4 times running, ending the game with probability 0.25 on each further pass would have ended 74% of big-board games early, about 61 plies sooner, and changed the eventual winner in 13% of those. A stopgap until the value head supports hard resignation: no model input or search change, so it comes out cleanly.
test: Implement in self-play and arena only, seeded for reproducible digests. Check the share of capped games and plies per game in a short run.

title: Find why stalling players repeat the exact same two points
why: In recorded games the side behind alternated between the same two coordinates for 150 plies, one on the 1/256 grid and one off it, which looks like snapping in candidate sampling. In a continuous game that means the move set there is effectively finite.
test: Trace candidate generation at one such position: which points are proposed, which survive snapping, and why the same two win. Related to the parked repetition policy (5b4efdee).

title: Fork the run from update 12 with the new recipe
why: Strength rose to update 11 or 12 and then fell about 20 Elo an update, and newer windows trained worse nets. The fork tests whether the value recipe, wider window and game-end change stop the decline. About 9 hours of generation.
test: After value-recipe and random-stop, run about 12 updates from update 12 and rate them on the 38 board against the original 12 to 23 curve.

title: Test the stones of previous positions as input
why: The net sees only the current position and whether the last move was a pass, so it cannot see a repetition. --history-plies adds the stones of N earlier positions in training only; the Rust raster does not render them yet.
test: 3 plies on the 450k recipe run, against the same run without history: held-out policy KL and value MSE. Adopting it needs the raster and inference to render the planes.

title: Rebuild and check the Rust side after the Fedora upgrade
why: The upgrade moved system Python to 3.15 and broke training/.venv, which was rebuilt on a uv-managed 3.14. The Rust binaries were not rebuilt or run since.
test: cargo build --release, then correctness/check.sh.

title: Report value MSE or log loss, not MAE
why: MAE ranked an overconfident value head best: stride-8 thinning read 0.56 MAE but 0.70 MSE against 0.59 MSE for 16 labels per game. The learner's selection score and logs use MAE.
test: Add value MSE and cross-entropy to evaluate(), and use one of them in the selection score.

title: Let komi follow the result per board
why: Black's self-play win rate fell to about 10% on small boards and 30% on big ones, and the fitted fair komi was often below the sampler's floor. Partly a game-end effect, so decide after random-stop.
test: Measure Black's win rate by board after random-stop, then widen the range or fit the centre from recent games.
